young.html: Jane Austen wrote six famous novels in England about 200 years ago. Emma is about a clever, kind-hearted, rather bossy young woman named Emma Woodhouse who loves playing matchmaker in her village.

There is just one problem: Emma is almost always wrong. She thinks the vicar loves her friend Harriet, but he really wants to marry Emma. She thinks a charming young man is in love with her, but he has a secret. And she never notices who really cares about her.

young.html: Along the way Emma makes a hurtful joke about a poor, kind older woman, and her friend Mr. Knightley tells her plainly that it was wrong. Emma feels terrible, and she changes. The book is funny, but it is also about learning to see other people truly and to be kind.

Match the clues. Emma jumped to conclusions. Play a detective game: one person acts out a short scene without words (for example, looking for lost keys), and everyone guesses what is going on. Was the first guess right? What clue did people miss?

full.html: Jane Austen (1775–1817), a clergyman's daughter, lived most of her life in country villages in the south of England. She published four novels in her lifetime, all anonymously, "By the Author of Pride and Prejudice" and so on; two more appeared after her death. Emma came out in December 1815 (dated 1816), dedicated, at his request, to the Prince Regent, who admired her books. She reportedly said she was creating a heroine whom no one but herself would much like.

full.text: Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence; and had lived nearly twenty-one years in the world with very little to distress or vex her.
full.author: Austen

full.html: Notice the word seemed. The opening sentence already hints that Emma's comfortable life will be tested.

Emma has just seen her governess, Miss Taylor, marry the widower Mr. Weston, and she takes credit for the match. Bored, she adopts a sweet young friend, Harriet Smith, and persuades her to refuse a good farmer, Robert Martin, so that she can marry the vicar, Mr. Elton. Mr. Elton, it turns out, wants Emma. Then Frank Churchill, Mr. Weston's charming son, arrives and flirts with Emma, while the quiet, gifted Jane Fairfax keeps her distance. Emma misreads everyone.

full.text: Mr. Knightley, in fact, was one of the few people who could see faults in Emma Woodhouse, and the only one who ever told her of them ...
full.author: Austen

full.html: At a picnic on Box Hill, Emma makes a joke at the expense of Miss Bates, a poor, good-natured, endlessly talkative older woman. Afterward Mr. Knightley takes her aside:

full.text: "She is poor; she has sunk from the comforts she was born to; and, if she live to old age, must probably sink more. Her situation should secure your compassion. It was badly done, indeed!"
full.author: Austen

full.html: Emma cries all the way home, and the next morning she visits Miss Bates to make amends. Soon the secrets come out: Frank has been engaged to Jane all along, and when Harriet confesses that she hopes Mr. Knightley loves her, Emma realizes, in a flash, that she loves him herself.

Austen tells the story mostly through Emma's own thoughts, in a style later called free indirect discourse: the narrator's voice slips into the character's way of seeing. So readers make Emma's mistakes along with her, and learn as she learns.
Reading Emma as only a romance. It is a comedy about judgment: how pride, boredom and wishful thinking lead a clever person to see what she wants to see.

items: Aristotle's Ethics, earlier on this ladder, says we become good by practice and correct our faults through friends who tell us the truth; Mr. Knightley is that kind of friend.
Shakespeare's comedies, such as Much Ado About Nothing, also turn on misreadings and matchmaking.
George Eliot's Middlemarch, later in this era, widens Austen's village into a whole town and its web of lives.
Sir Walter Scott, reviewing Emma in 1815–16, praised Austen for making ordinary life interesting.
Why is it so easy to see what we want to see?
What makes a good friend: someone who agrees with you, or someone who tells you the truth?
Is it ever right to arrange other people's lives for them?
How should we treat people who have less money or status than we do?

questions: Have you ever been sure about something and then found out you were wrong?
Mr. Knightley told Emma a hard truth. Is that kind or unkind? Why?
Why do you think Emma made fun of Miss Bates? How did she make it right?
Is it a good idea to try to choose friends or partners for other people?
Which character in Emma would you most like to meet?
